Seems to me that a whole bunch of problems regarding immigrants or visitors to a country could be pretty simply solved by requiring liability and medical insurance and having them pay their way for any services they use.

This would tend to keep criminals out (insurance would be too high, and restitution would get paid anyways if there was an incident), while allowing businesses and workers to create wealth and prosperity that would benefit society at large.

Seems to me that the political left should love this idea, as the most in need (desperate immigrants) could make a living and send money back to those in dire need (their families). Diversity would increase. If they didn't have the money for insurance up-front they could be sponsored by a range of groups (business, left-leaning, right-leaning, etc.) and be paid back as they built their life.

Well the ones that are healthy and non-criminal would (many employers would cover this and take the insurance payments out of pay), and those who don't meet the criteria wouldn't. Seems like a win-win to me.

There's a general problem with it, however. Immigrants who come from economically equivalent societies are not a problem. Immigrants from economically inferior societies, however, will be willing to work for less than "locally fair" wages. This means immigration, if not checked, can overrun a local economy with workers who are willing to work for far less than the former market wage.

As a consequence of this, native workers can find themselves without jobs. This can be because they have less compact or supportive familial groups, or individuals who have no support groups as immigrant families tend to. Meaning they can reinforce locally lowered wages, which reinforce the societal model of clustered familial groups. In other words, this can further impact the local culture, by forcing a formerly individualistic society to revert back to a more clustered familial group. Ever hear "Why don't you just get a job" from your parents? Anybody? They could - you can't (in this hypothetical example).

The ultimate problem is one of gentrification. Is the gentrification going to be beneficial, or harmful? I argue it can be decidedly harmful specifically against individuals with support groups that cannot compete. It can result in the native population having to accept lower standards of life, as the population of immigrants from economically inferior societies increases.

The notion that immigration is harmful is one the political left has been ignoring. However, it is a very real problem, and a very frightening one for native populations. While the capitalists may love it, for it cheapens labor, it inherently will reduce quality of life closer to that quality of life the immigrants came from. This can also be how you get closed communities, where only one ethnic group exists, because it out-competed native groups in a race to the bottom. Resulting in a localized economy equivalent to their native conditions - and demonstrably worse.

I've always wanted to try DnD, but was never thrilled about trying to meet with a group of strangers to "guide" me along.

I recently found out a few people I know are all at least somewhat interested in playing as well (or at the very least aren't opposed to trying it out). We have a group of 5-6 people who have never played DnD, all with varying degrees of interest. We bought the Starter Set and started to read through it a little but feel completely overwhelmed.

Any tips on how a group of newbies can get started? Does one person just have to power through the reading and explain it to the rest or are there videos or something online that make it a little easier?

Any help is appreciated!
Group of new players trying to learn

Lucky for you there are many sources and methods to get acquainted! My suggestions:

  • Get a DM or decide who among your group is going to DM. DM is a Dungeon master and basically runs the game.

  • If reading is your thing, I recommend checking out Wizard's free stuff to read on their website

  • Everyone should be somewhat familiar with the material. It makes everything smoother and if everyone is giving input, it will show.

  • Keep it simple. Keep it fun. This is your first game.

  • Pick a day and a time and get your party going. The hardest part I find is getting everyone together.

  • So geekandsundry have a show called critical role and features voice actors playing D&D. While maybe not the best example, there is one video that does a good job of showing and explaining the basics of D&D.

Hope this helps.

5-6 people is a perfect group, especially if you are all on the same level :) As /u/Fishy_Old_Guy said, the hardest part tends to be getting everyone together at the same time to play. Later on you can setup rules for how to handle missing players but I would personally recommend having all present for the first several sessions so that no one falls behind during the critical learning periods.

The Dungeon Master (DM)
I would definitely start with selecting a DM; this can be anyone but the more creative and organized people tend to fall into the role better. The DM should have a copy of the players handbook (ideally, the starter set stuff will work fine for a while until things get too complicated), pens, pencils and paper. They should also read through most of the Lost Mines of Phandelver DM guide so they have a good idea of how the story plays out. They don't have to read the whole thing at once, but having run it myself, you should at least be a few chapters ahead so that you can be ready if the players make an unexpected leap in the story (trust me it will happen). The DM will need to know the very basics of the attack rolls, damage rolls, spellcasting, and ability checks so that they can explain it to the players.

The Players
Since you have the starter set, I would totally recommend sticking with the pre-made characters. Have the players pick through the character sheets and then get familiar with their characters (health, abilities, spells, etc). Most of the starter set characters are easy to start right off with except for the Wizard and the Cleric as those players will have to have a general idea of how spellcasting works; they should be given a chance to collude together with the DM to establish the basic principles.

First Session
Remember that it is a game and as long as people are laughing and having a good time, you are doing it right. Bring lots of booze and snacks to help with this :) . The first session should just start off from the book as it very expertly guides the DM and players through the basics at a reasonable pace.

For the players: be patient with the DM as they will have to consult the guide every few minutes to ensure they know what to do next and that everyone is following the rules properly. Each session will get progressively faster and smoother as you go. Just have fun, drink your beer, and be ready to learn stuff as you go.

For the DM: take your time and let the players do what they want to do. They will ALWAYS deviate from the story and they will NEVER do what you expect; and that is more than okay, it is DnD. It will take time to get used to playing things by ear and rolling with the situation. Just let things happen and guide your players from afar. Don't be afraid to improvise and change things on the fly if you think the players will have fun with it; just make sure you have the basic plot points down so you don't accidentally throw the main story off course as that can be tricky to come back from. You will absolutely misunderstand a few rules and will probably be doing something wrong for a few sessions until you our a player points it out later on; just make sure that if you update something that you tell everyone ahead of time. If you don't know what to do and you don't want to interrupt the session, you can just make a ruling and tell the players that "we will do x for now until I have a chance to look over this." Then review the issue and let players know before starting the next session.

I can't praise the starter set any more for doing its job; everything in there is designed to teach new players and DMs everything sequentially. There is a pretty good video series Here which goes over the whole starter set; there are obviously spoilers so only the DM should watch it though. Good luck, have fun and don't be afraid to ask questions here in /v/dnd :)

How does the ISS stay in perfect orbit around the earth without the gravitational pull of the earth pulling it into the atmosphere?
It doesn't - the ISS has thrusters that are used to compensate for the effects of gravity and friction as well as general orbital adjustments.

Try reading up on newton's cannonball (Wikipedia article, has some good animations).
Basically, you know how if you throw a ball it curves downward before it hits the ground? Well if you get that ball moving fast enough, that arc will be the same (or greater then) the curvature of the earth. Of course, you can't do this at low alitudes because air resistance will slow the ball to the point at which it will fall normally, but the "air" is so thin in low earth orbit that it takes many months for enough slowing to occur to force re-entry.

I've read a great many books about Wicca, but I have not successfully practiced it myself. For example, I feel a bit silly when trying to cleanse and consecrate candles for candle magick because I feel nothing, see nothing, and am unaware of any changes that may have occurred. I face similar challenges when trying to perform other rituals or even just working on opening and closing the chakras. I visualize the energy that I am trying to work with, but I honestly feel nothing happening. I think I may be magically-impaired, really.

My next door neighbor is a high priestess and my SO practices the Golden Dawn and their experience when working magick are vastly different from mine. My neighbor tells of feeling the energies as she directs them where she needs them to go, and my SO perceives changes in his vision during some rituals (as well as experiencing/performing other things like astral projection, etc.). I, on the other hand, can't even judge a person's character with ANY accuracy (my mother has a knack for being able to instantly ascertain a person's character upon meeting them) and it's laughable how incorrect I am when trying those psychic cards where you predict what card will come next.

So.....what is practicing Wicca supposed to feel like? How do you know that you have accomplished something after you complete a ritual/spell?
